promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In which decade did minimalism first emerge as a style in the USA?
questions.explain: Minimalism developed in the United States during the 1960s with composers such as Riley, Reich and Glass.

questions.q: Which composer is most closely associated with minimalism?
questions.explain: Steve Reich is a leading minimalist, known for works such as Clapping Music and Music for 18 Musicians.

questions.q: Who pioneered the twelve-tone (serialist) technique in the early 1920s?
questions.explain: Arnold Schoenberg devised the twelve-tone method of composing with a fixed ordering of all twelve chromatic pitches.

questions.q: Expressionism in music is associated with which group of composers?
questions.explain: Expressionism is linked to the Second Viennese School of Schoenberg, Berg and Webern.

questions.q: What does the vocal technique 'Sprechgesang' involve?
options: A style halfway between speaking and singing
questions.explain: Sprechgesang ('spoken song') is a delivery between speech and song, famously used in Schoenberg's Pierrot Lunaire.

questions.q: Which 1964 work by Terry Riley is a landmark of early minimalism?
questions.explain: Terry Riley's In C (1964) is built from repeated short cells and is a foundational minimalist piece.

questions.q: The 'prepared piano', altering the sound by placing objects on or between the strings, was pioneered by which composer?
questions.explain: John Cage developed the prepared piano, inserting screws, bolts and rubber to create new percussive timbres.

questions.q: How many different pitches make up a tone row in serialism?
questions.explain: A serial tone row orders all twelve pitches of the chromatic scale before any is repeated.

questions.q: What best describes the minimalist technique of 'phasing'?
options: Two identical patterns start together then gradually shift out of alignment
The tempo slows continuously to a stop
All instruments play a single sustained chord
questions.explain: In phasing, identical repeating parts begin in unison and slowly move out of sync, creating shifting textures.

questions.q: What happens in the minimalist 'additive process'?
options: Notes are gradually added to a repeating pattern to lengthen it
The dynamics suddenly jump from quiet to loud
The key changes on every bar
Instruments drop out one by one until silence
questions.explain: Additive process expands a cell by progressively adding notes, so the pattern grows over time.

questions.q: What does it mean for a piece to be 'atonal'?
options: It has no home key or tonal centre
It is played without any instruments
questions.explain: Atonal music avoids a tonal centre, treating all twelve pitches as equal and often sounding dissonant.

questions.q: Which set of features is most characteristic of expressionist music?
options: Extreme emotion, harsh dissonance and angular melodies
Gentle consonance and simple folk tunes
Steady dance rhythms and clear major keys
Long lyrical melodies with lush Romantic harmony
questions.explain: Expressionism conveys intense inner emotion through dissonance, wide leaps and distorted, angular lines.

questions.q: In serialism, the 'retrograde' of a tone row is the row played how?
options: Backwards, from last note to first
questions.explain: The retrograde presents the original row's pitches in reverse order.

questions.q: What is the 'inversion' of a tone row?
options: The row with its intervals turned upside down
The row transposed up an octave
The row played twice as loud
questions.explain: In inversion, each ascending interval of the original becomes descending and vice versa.

questions.q: What is the role of an ostinato in much minimalist music?
options: A repeated pattern that provides a driving, hypnotic foundation
A free, improvised solo with no pulse
questions.explain: Repeating ostinato patterns underpin minimalism, giving its characteristic pulsing, hypnotic drive.

options: Spreading a melody across different instruments and timbres
Playing every note as loudly as possible
questions.explain: Klangfarbenmelodie ('tone-colour melody') distributes a line among instruments so timbre itself becomes melodic.

questions.q: A composer loops a short cell and slowly adds one extra note each time so the phrase gradually lengthens. Which technique is this?
questions.explain: Gradually adding notes to lengthen a repeating cell is the minimalist additive process.

questions.q: Two players perform the same rhythmic pattern, but one very gradually moves a beat ahead, producing a shimmering, shifting effect. Which technique is being used?
questions.explain: Identical parts drifting gradually out of alignment to create shifting textures is phasing.

questions.q: A composer takes the inversion of a tone row and then plays it in reverse order. Which transformation results?
questions.explain: Playing the inverted row backwards produces the retrograde inversion, one of serialism's four standard forms.
